title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI (Latent Space podcast)
author: swyx / Basil Chatha (hosts); guest Jeff Barg
paywall: none (show notes and full auto-transcript on page)
what_changed: Production retrospective from Clay's Head of AI on rebuilding its tool-loop agent as a coding agent, running agents at per-row scale, model routing, when to post-train, and the unsolved problem of agents debugging agent traces.
mechanism: Sculptor v1 (Sept 2025, Sonnet 3.5 era) was a fixed set of tools in a loop with a heavily tuned system prompt: good at adding columns, bad at booking ten qualified meetings. Evals used an LLM judge on WHICH TOOLS were called, which missed real usage (asking it to analyze a table; enterprise tables with millions of rows). Lessons: coding agents are very good at Bash/Python; composed narrow tools were too limited; the agent could not see CRM/campaign results. Rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness running the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox, plus a data layer ('Audiences') that entity-matches records across CRM and Gong so the agent sees them together. Infra is hand-rolled: BullMQ for agent jobs (no Temporal, no LangGraph), Postgres + ClickHouse for product data, Snowflake for analytics. Scale problem: users run an agent per row, so a 50,000-row run spikes inference all at once; they added LangSmith for observability, request throttling, and pause/resume when a provider goes down or rate-limits, and per-tenant fairness so a 10-person workflow still runs while an enterprise enriches 1M rows (noisy neighbor). No dual-sourcing/fallback of inference providers yet ('we'll probably do this now'). Model choice: customers hate the model selector; Clay is launching an automatic per-task router but keeping the selector for power users/agencies.
evidence_quality: Practitioner first-hand account; numbers are the guest's own (napkin math, internal evals not published). No metrics on router or agent success rates.
independent_confirmation: Funding ($115M at $7.1B, Sept) linked in show notes; technical claims single-source.
relevance: High: concrete agent-ops lessons (LLM-judge on tool-call choice misses real usage; per-row agent fan-out needs throttling, pause/resume and fairness; CLI + sandbox beats bespoke tool loop; post-training threshold; trace debugging still manual).

title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
author: Lance Martin, Jake Eaton, Arvin Aminpour, Emma Webb, Bharat Mediratta, Ravi Trivedi
event_date: Migration work April to September 2026 (public traffic moved to Rust in September 2026)
what_changed: Anthropic describes how it rewrote the Python Messages API (serving all Claude tokens incl. Claude Code, Cowork) in Rust using agents, and how it verified parity by turning the production API into an oracle via privacy-preserving shadow traffic, checkpoint diffs, bug fingerprints and three agent verification loops.
mechanism: Shadowing with model output replayed (model run once, output replayed to Rust, so nondeterminism and double-billing avoided). Step-by-step checkpoint comparison (accept/reject, resolve settings, build prompt; piece-by-piece within the prompt). Fingerprint record per diff (step, prompt piece, first differing byte, byte lengths of each side) with no user text. Script every 10-30 min groups records by differing fields; coordinating Claude agent alerted only on new record kinds, assigns a worker agent per kind and opens a Slack thread for humans. Inner loop: cloud sandbox with both codebases, sub-second local input check (build prompt in both, never call model) plus output check against a fake model with scripted replies; agent hypothesizes from fingerprint, writes its own request to reproduce, edits Rust until match, adds a test failing on old/passing on new. Seam: human PR review before outer loop. Outer loop: deploy, compare fingerprint frequency on builds with/without fix, stratified by logged request features (model, caching, tools, extended thinking). Memory loop: reviewer corrections saved as notes/rules (CLAUDE.md), searches for same mistake, tests, lints, and a merge check requiring matching Rust change for any Python change (or exemption).
evidence_quality: First-party, detailed, with figures (match-rate over time, CPU/memory/TTFT panels, merge counts). Numbers are self-reported; no external replication.
independent_confirmation: Partially: Katelyn Lesse (Anthropic platform eng lead) describes the same migration on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nov 25 (same org, so not independent). Podcast says 'around five months', consistent with April to September.
relevance: High. Directly actionable pattern for agent-driven migrations: verification (not generation) as bottleneck, production as oracle, privacy-preserving diff fingerprints, layered inner/outer/memory loops, and a concrete reward-hacking example (agent copied web-search tool description into static files to make prompts match; human rejected it).
overlap_with_prior: Not in prior_urls. Touches recurring themes (Edition 3 'check a record it can't edit', Edition 4 'audit the grader', Pragmatic Engineer software factories) but is new material. Outside slice B's roster (Anthropic is a lab source) so may also be picked up by the labs slice; included because the roster podcast links to it as the primary source.

title: How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling
author: Atharva Joshi
event_date: 2026-11-25; optimization merged into FlashInfer main
what_changed: Optimized SageAttention3 NVFP4 attention kernel for SM120 (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) up to 1.64x faster kernel latency; merged into FlashInfer; Reactor reports up to 15.34% end-to-end latency reduction serving world models.
mechanism: Original CTA (4 producer + 8 consumer warps) runs QK, online softmax + NVFP4 probability quantization, PV serially per N128 tile, leaving Tensor Cores idle; registers at ~95.3% (62,464). Fix: split each N128 score tile into two N64 register slots; once a half is exponentiated and quantized, its registers are reused for the next tile's QK half, overlapping next-tile MMA with current softmax/PV without a second score buffer. SM120 MMA constrained to m16n8k64 so k=128 needs two MMAs.
evidence_quality: First-party with partner (Reactor) production numbers; kernel-level detail.
independent_confirmation: Code merged upstream in FlashInfer (claimed).
relevance: Low-medium for this newsletter (kernel-level; relevant to teams self-hosting on RTX PRO 6000 / sm120). Pairs with HF Inkling hill-climb on same GPU.
reason: Kernel-level optimization for a narrow audience.

title: How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? An Empirical Study of Unneeded Edits in Repository-Level Agent Patches
author: Aakash Goel, Benjamin Steenhoek, Yu Hu
event_date: Submitted 2026-11-25; announced in arXiv listing Thu 26 Nov 2026 (confirmed on abs page and listing)
what_changed: Introduces Delta Residue Attribution (DRA) and finds that larger agent patches are mostly tests/docs (on SWE-bench Verified), with agent code at least as 'necessary' as developer code; ~11% of agent code units still unneeded.
mechanism: DRA replays a resolved trajectory, splits the final patch into independently revertible units, traces each unit to the step that wrote it (labelled by role: explore/reproduce/fix etc.), reverts each unit and reruns task tests (delta debugging) to decide necessity; necessity precision NP_code = share of needed code units. Behavioral probes check unneeded code; developer patches graded the same way.
evidence_quality: Large sample: 7,660 resolved GitHub Copilot CLI trajectories across 18 frontier models (6,728 SWE-bench Verified, 932 DeepSWE); pre-registered hypotheses with listed deviations. Test-based necessity inherits test-overfitting caveat.
independent_confirmation: None; single preprint, not peer reviewed.
relevance: High: gives harness builders a concrete pruning method and numbers on self-audit vs test-based pruning; reframes 'agents over-edit' claims.

title: The Best Defense Against This Wave of AI Attacks: Hack Yourself First (Try This Now)
author: Cole Medin
organization: Cole Medin (YouTube); tool shown is Cloudflare's security-audit skill
what_changed: A practitioner walkthrough of running Cloudflare's open-source security-audit coding-agent skill against your own repo before attackers' agents do, then proving and fixing what it finds.
mechanism: Linked repo github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill (MIT; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com): six-phase audit run by isolated agents: (1) Reconnaissance writes architecture.md and coverage-ledger.json (trust boundaries, input surfaces, deterministic coverage); (2) coverage-led hunting with isolated hunters assigned from ledger units plus 'coverage critics' to find gaps; (3) every unique candidate goes to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it; (4) structured output to findings.json validated against report-schema.json with three verdicts: confirmed (complete source trace + bounded observed result), needs_validation (exact unresolved fact, no severity), rejected; (5) independent record verification by fresh agents; (6) target-neutral reports REPORT.md / FINDINGS-DETAIL.md / NEEDS-VALIDATION.md. Zero-dependency Node validators validate-coverage-ledger.cjs and validate-findings.cjs run after each ledger update and in Phases 4-5. Per-class hunting files include AI-AND-LLM.md (prompt injection, agent/tool, output handling), SUPPLY-CHAIN-AND-RELEASE.md, CLOUD-AND-DEPLOYMENT.md, DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE.md, RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION (incl. operator spend), etc. Install: npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill --skill security-audit [--global]. Trigger phrases like 'security audit this codebase'. Default output dir ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>; writes inside the target repo only if you pick a VCS-ignored dir. Requires an OS-enforced sandbox (no external network, sanitized allowlisted env, resource limits, writes only to scratch paths) to execute target code; without it leads stay needs_validation. Runs are additive: prior ledgers/findings target gaps and revalidate changed source. Design principles: only confirm established boundary failures; the checking agent is never the finding agent; severity = likelihood x impact; defense-in-depth gaps are hardening notes not vulns; 'a single run found roughly half of the vulnerabilities that repeated runs found in total'.
evidence_quality: Video content beyond chapter titles UNVERIFIED (YouTube page not readable by fetch; only RSS description). Skill details confirmed from the repo README. Background: Cloudflare blog 'Build your own vulnerability harness' (2026-06-18, https://blog.cloudflare.com/build-your-own-vulnerability-harness) says the skill was ~450 lines and seeded their fleet-wide harness; three walls they hit: context exhaustion (fixed by externalizing state, LLM as stateless compute), persistence across crashes, cross-repo reasoning; advice: minimal harness = Recon, Hunt, Validate stages in a database plus a separate Validator that can't file its own findings; vary models between discovery and validation.
independent_confirmation: Repo README and Cloudflare June blog are primary sources; Cole's results on his own project are single-author demo (UNVERIFIED).
relevance: High: actionable this week; directly continues Edition 5's agent-security thread with a defender-side, verifier-separated audit loop.
